2 Methods

The subsections below are written as manuscript prose and are intended to be moved into the Methods section of the paper with minimal editing. They are deliberately self-contained: nothing in them depends on having read the rest of this report.

2.1 Data source

We analysed the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project (HCUP) Nationwide Readmissions Database (NRD) for discharge years 2016 to 2022. The NRD is a nationally representative all-payer administrative database constructed from HCUP State Inpatient Databases in participating states, containing verified patient linkage numbers that permit a patient to be tracked across hospitals within a single calendar year. It does not link patients across calendar years, does not contain geographic identifiers below the level of the nation, and does not contain a race or ethnicity variable; none of these limitations can be circumvented and each is addressed explicitly in the Limitations. Discharge weights supplied with the data, together with the sampling stratum and the hospital identifier, were used to produce nationally representative estimates. The Nationwide Readmissions Database contains de-identified, publicly available administrative data and this analysis was therefore determined to be non-human-subjects research and exempt from institutional review board review. The HCUP Data Use Agreement was executed before any data were accessed. Reporting follows STROBE, with the RECORD extension for routinely collected health data.

2.2 Cohort

We identified all adult hospitalizations with an any-listed ICD-10-PCS code for percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion with an intraluminal device (02L73DK). Discharges coded with an extraluminal device (02L73CK) or with an unspecified device (02L73ZK) were excluded from the cohort definition: these denote different procedures with different complication profiles, and their number is reported in the cohort flow. We then excluded hospitalizations of patients younger than 18 years; hospitalizations ending in in-hospital death, because a decedent cannot be readmitted; hospitalizations ending in transfer to another short-term acute care hospital, because the discharge does not end the episode of care and a subsequent admission would be an artefact of the transfer; December discharges, because NRD linkage does not cross calendar years and a 30-day window would be incomplete by construction; records without the identifiers required for linkage; and hospitalizations with concomitant coronary artery bypass grafting, a surgical or transcatheter valve procedure, or an open or thoracoscopic left atrial appendage operation, because these change length of stay and the complication structure entirely. All code lists are published in full in the supplement. Analyses were performed at the level of the hospitalization; a small number of patients contributed more than one qualifying admission within a calendar year, and restricting to the first such admission per patient-year is a pre-specified sensitivity analysis.

2.3 Exposure

The exposure was dialysis-dependent kidney failure, defined as the conjunction of an any-listed ICD-10-CM diagnosis of end-stage renal disease (N18.6) and at least one marker of dialysis dependence: dependence on renal dialysis (Z99.2), an encounter for fitting, adjustment or adequacy testing of a dialysis catheter (Z49.01, Z49.02, Z49.31, Z49.32), performance of urinary filtration (5A1D60Z, 5A1D70Z, 5A1D80Z), or peritoneal dialysis (3E1M39Z). The code 5A1D90Z, which denotes continuous urinary filtration for more than 18 hours per day, was deliberately not treated as a marker of dialysis dependence: it identifies continuous renal replacement therapy in a critically ill patient with acute kidney injury rather than maintenance dialysis, and including it would contaminate the exposed arm and invert the clinical meaning of the exposure. Requiring both components is what makes the exposure dialysis dependence rather than coded kidney failure; the wider definition, an N18.6 diagnosis with or without a dialysis marker, is reported as a pre-specified sensitivity analysis.

2.4 Outcomes

The primary outcome was all-cause readmission to any hospital within 30 days of discharge from the index hospitalization. Secondary outcomes, forming a single pre-specified family, were: readmission with a bleeding principal diagnosis (AHRQ DXCCSR category DIG021, or an intracranial haemorrhage code I60-I62, or acute posthaemorrhagic anaemia D62); readmission with an ischaemic stroke principal diagnosis (DXCCSR CIR020); unplanned (non-elective) readmission; in-hospital death during the readmission; pericardial effusion or tamponade during the index hospitalization; pericardial drainage during the index hospitalization; and non-home discharge from the index hospitalization. Acute kidney injury during the index hospitalization is reported descriptively in the unexposed arm only: on a maintenance-dialysis background an N17 code does not carry its usual meaning and a between-arm comparison would be uninterpretable rather than merely imprecise. Index in-hospital mortality is reported on the full procedural cohort, before the discharge-survivor restriction, because that is the only denominator on which it is interpretable. Costs were obtained by multiplying total charges by the HCUP hospital-specific cost-to-charge ratio and were inflation-adjusted to 2022 US dollars using the CPI-U, All Items, U.S. city average, not seasonally adjusted, annual average (BLS series CUUR0000SA0).

2.5 Statistical analysis

All analyses accounted for the complex survey design using the discharge weight, the sampling stratum and the hospital as the primary sampling unit. Because stratum and hospital identifiers are re-issued in each data year and do not refer to the same unit across years, year-unique stratum and cluster identifiers were constructed before the design was specified; a single survey design object was built once on the complete cohort and every subsequent analysis was taken as a subset of it, so that stratum information required for variance estimation was never discarded. Strata containing a single primary sampling unit were centred at the grand mean rather than dropped.

Baseline characteristics are reported as design-weighted percentages with unweighted counts, and are compared using standardized mean differences rather than p-values, because in a cohort of this size every p-value would be small and none would describe the magnitude of an imbalance.

The primary model was a survey-weighted logistic regression of 30-day all-cause readmission on dialysis-dependent kidney failure. Age was modelled as a restricted cubic spline rather than as a linear or categorical term. The covariate block was deliberately compact and fixed a priori: sex, primary expected payer, ZIP-code median income quartile, NCHS urban-rural residence, admission type, hospital bed size, hospital location and teaching status, discharge year, hospital left atrial appendage occlusion volume tertile computed within year on the full procedural population before exclusions, the components of the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score, the bleeding-relevant components of HAS-BLED, and a residual Elixhauser comorbidity count. Renal failure was excluded from that count because it is collinear with the exposure by construction, and so was every comorbidity entered individually, so that no comorbidity contributes twice. No stepwise or data-driven variable selection was performed at any point.

Because 30-day readmission is common in this population, odds ratios materially overstate risk ratios, so adjusted absolute risks were obtained by marginal standardization (g-computation) over the observed covariate distribution of the whole analytic cohort, with variance by the delta method on the design-based covariance matrix and t critical values on the design degrees of freedom. A propensity-score overlap-weighted (ATO) estimate was treated as co-primary rather than as a sensitivity analysis: it reduces the outcome model to a single exposure term while balancing the full covariate set through the propensity score, which is the appropriate response to a study whose exposed arm is small. The outcome model was refitted on the overlap-weighted design, making that estimator doubly robust; the design-based variance treats the estimated weights as fixed, which is standard practice and mildly conservative for overlap weights.

An E-value was computed on the risk ratio scale to quantify the strength of unmeasured confounding that would be required to explain the finding. A pre-specified negative control outcome with no plausible causal link to the exposure was analysed using the identical model. Secondary outcomes were adjusted for multiplicity within their pre-specified family using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure; the primary outcome was tested once, unadjusted, and is the only confirmatory test in the paper. Sensitivity analyses were not multiplicity-corrected and are judged on movement of the point estimate. Subgroup analyses were exploratory, were assessed by design-based interaction tests rather than by comparing subgroup confidence intervals, and are not reported in the Conclusions. Cells representing fewer than 11 unweighted discharges are suppressed throughout in accordance with the HCUP Data Use Agreement. Analyses were performed in R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24 ucrt) using the survey package version 4.5.

All percentages are design-based national estimates with 95% confidence intervals from the survey design; the figure in parentheses after the interval is the unweighted event count. Readmission, procedural complications, length of stay, cost and disposition are computed on the index cohort (discharge survivors with a complete 30-day window and no concomitant cardiac surgery); in-hospital mortality is computed on the full LAAO cohort, which retains in-hospital deaths, because that is the only denominator on which a mortality rate is interpretable. The two denominators are reported separately and are never mixed. Readmission characteristics are computed on index admissions that were followed by a readmission. A binary outcome with fewer than 11 unweighted events or non-events in either arm is suppressed in every arm and in every table, so that no suppressed count can be recovered by subtraction (suppressed here: Ischaemic stroke readmission; In-hospital death at index). ACUTE KIDNEY INJURY IS REPORTED IN THE UNEXPOSED ARM ONLY (Table 2d): on a maintenance-dialysis background an N17 code does not carry its usual meaning, and a between-arm comparison of it would be uninterpretable rather than merely imprecise. These are unadjusted comparisons; the adjusted estimates are in Table 3.

The primary model is a survey-weighted logistic regression of 30-day all-cause readmission on dialysis-dependent kidney failure, adjusted for the pre-specified compact covariate block: age modelled as a restricted cubic spline with four knots, sex, primary payer, ZIP-code income quartile, NCHS urban-rural residence, admission type, hospital bed size, location and teaching status, discharge year, hospital LAAO volume tertile, the CHA₂DS₂-VASc components (heart failure, hypertension, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA/thromboembolism, vascular disease), the HAS-BLED-adjacent components (prior major bleeding, liver disease, alcohol use disorder, anaemia), and a residual Elixhauser comorbidity count. The full 31-flag Elixhauser set is deliberately NOT used: with this exposed event count it would produce unstable estimates, and the clinically relevant comorbidities are entered individually instead. Renal failure is excluded from the comorbidity count by pre-specification because it is collinear with the exposure by construction. Adjusted absolute risks were obtained by marginal standardization over the whole analytic cohort with delta-method variance on the design-based covariance matrix and t critical values on 1996 design degrees of freedom. No pre-specified covariate required removal by the sparse-cell guard. The overlap-weighted estimate in Table 3b is a CO-PRIMARY estimator in this study rather than a sensitivity analysis, because it reduces the outcome model to a single exposure term while balancing the full covariate set through the propensity score. The effective sample size after overlap weighting was 7,864, and 0 of 20 covariates retained an absolute standardized mean difference of 0.10 or more. Sequential Models 1 to 4 are NOT monotone – check whether a covariate has been misclassified as a mediator. Model 5 is OVER-ADJUSTED: the Model 4 to Model 5 change is attenuation consistent with mediation and is not an adjusted estimate. All secondary outcomes are exploratory and form one Benjamini-Hochberg family (adjusted over the 6 outcome(s) with at least 11 events and non-events in each arm); the primary outcome is not a member of it.

E-value. An unmeasured confounder would need to be associated with both dialysis-dependent kidney failure and 30-day readmission by a risk ratio of at least 3.58 each, above and beyond the measured covariates, to explain away the observed adjusted risk ratio of 2.08; to move the confidence limit closest to the null to 1.00 the required association is 3.17. The most plausible such confounders here are frailty and dialysis vintage, neither of which the Nationwide Readmissions Database records in any form.

EXPLORATORY. Based on 7,909 unweighted 30-day readmissions with a recorded principal diagnosis, mapped to the AHRQ DXCCSR v2025.1 default inpatient category. 3 readmission principal diagnosis code(s) had no default CCSR assignment and are grouped under ‘Other’. The top 4 categories by overall weighted share are reported – four rather than ten or fifteen because this cohort has a thin exposed arm; the number was fixed in the analysis plan before any result was seen. All remaining categories are folded into ‘Other’, as are 1 category that fell below the 11 unweighted discharge threshold in at least one exposure arm (Heart failure). Percentages are within-arm shares of all readmissions in that arm and sum to 100% down each column. P values are design-based Wald tests from survey-weighted logistic regression of the category indicator on exposure; q values are Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted across the reported categories, a family separate from the secondary-outcome family.

This is a cumulative incidence curve for the first readmission among discharge survivors, not a survival curve. Death after discharge is not observed in the Nationwide Readmissions Database and is an uncontrollable competing risk; because post-discharge mortality is substantially higher in dialysis-dependent patients, that competing risk attenuates the observed difference between arms rather than inflating it.

ALL SUBGROUP RESULTS ARE EXPLORATORY and are not adjusted for multiplicity. Each estimate is the adjusted association between dialysis-dependent kidney failure and 30-day readmission, refitted within that subgroup using the primary covariate block. A stratum is reported only when each of its four exposure-by-outcome cells holds at least 11 unweighted discharges; the interaction p value is derived from every stratum and is suppressed whenever any stratum is. Effect modification is assessed by a design-based Wald test on the whole interaction block, fitted on the rows with a non-missing modifier; the modifier’s deterministic parent covariate is removed from that model so that no coefficient is aliased (prior major bleeding for the bleeding subgroup, the volume tertile for the volume subgroup). Non-overlapping subgroup confidence intervals are NOT evidence of interaction and are not interpreted as such. The prior-major-bleeding subgroup is the pre-specified restricted comparison that addresses indication bias directly. No subgroup finding appears in the Conclusions.

Four qualifications apply to every trend result reported here and must appear alongside them in the manuscript. First, these are seven independent annual cross-sections drawn from a partly changing hospital sample, not a longitudinal cohort; NRD patient linkage does not cross calendar years and hospital identifiers are reset each year. Second, coding intensity increased across this window, so an apparent rise in the prevalence of an any-listed diagnosis reflects ascertainment as much as incidence, and no biological trend is claimed. Third, 2020 is anomalous because of pandemic admission avoidance, COVID-19 coding and capacity effects, and is examined in the leave-2020-out sensitivity analysis S2. Fourth, and specific to this procedure, left atrial appendage occlusion diffused rapidly across this window, so the annual volume series describes the adoption of a technology rather than the incidence of a disease, and because ICD-10-PCS does not identify the device model the later years are a mixture of device generations in unknown proportion. The trend test enters discharge year as a continuous term replacing the year factor, which is a design-based test; Joinpoint and segmented regression on the annual point estimates are not appropriate because they ignore the survey design. An exposure-by-year interaction was NOT tested in this study: the analysis plan restricts that test to the two larger studies in the programme, and with this exposed event count spread over seven years it would be an underpowered test whose null result would carry no information.

Sensitivity analyses are consistency checks and are NOT corrected for multiplicity; they are judged on whether the point estimate moves, not on whether a p-value crosses 0.05. Every subset was taken with subset() on the survey design constructed once on the full cohort, so the stratum information needed for correct variance estimation is preserved; the design was never rebuilt on filtered data. S3 is the co-primary overlap-weighted estimate carried across from Table 3b, not a second computation of it. S5 is a CALENDAR restriction, not a device restriction: ICD-10-PCS code 02L73DK covers every intraluminal left atrial appendage occlusion device and the device model cannot be identified from administrative data. S6 widens the exposure to any N18.6 diagnosis regardless of dialysis dependence, which is closer to the definition used by the published propensity-matched network analysis. S8 re-ascertains the exposure within the diagnosis and procedure fields present in every data year; records exposed only through a higher-numbered field are re-classified as unexposed. Present-on-admission-restricted definitions are NOT ESTIMABLE in NRD 2016-2022, which carries no present-on-admission indicator. Rows that could not be estimated or were suppressed (reason in the table): Present-on-admission-restricted definitions (SAP C1 item 4). The overlap-weighted design had an effective sample size of 7,864. The Cox model in S4 is a sensitivity analysis only and is not an alternative primary specification: every patient has complete 30-day follow-up by design, so a hazard ratio adds no information beyond the binary outcome.

Variance inflation factors are computed per design-matrix column rather than aggregated to a generalized VIF, which is the conservative reading: if no individual dummy column is inflated then no multi-level factor is either. The c-statistic is survey-weighted and tie-corrected. The calibration test is the survey analogue of the Hosmer-Lemeshow test and is NOT the Archer-Lemeshow F-adjusted mean residual test; it should not be described as such. Singleton strata were centred at the grand mean (survey.lonely.psu = ‘adjust’) rather than removed; 59 stratum/strata contained a single primary sampling unit, which is expected for a concentrated procedure whose year-specific hospital identifiers cannot be pooled. All manually constructed intervals use t critical values on 1,996 design degrees of freedom rather than 1.96.

6 Limitations

The unit of analysis is the hospitalization, not the patient. The NRD contains verified within-year patient linkage, and a minority of patients contributed more than one qualifying admission in a calendar year. The pre-specified first-admission-per-patient-year sensitivity analysis addresses this and is reported in Table 6.

Follow-up cannot cross a calendar year. NRD linkage is within-year only, so December discharges were excluded by design. The consequence is that the cohort under-represents late-December activity, and no 30-day window that would straddle 31 December is observable in this data source at all.

Post-discharge death is not observed. The database records in-hospital death but nothing that happens outside a hospital, so death after discharge is an uncontrollable competing risk for readmission. This matters more here than in most readmission studies: post-discharge mortality is substantially higher in dialysis-dependent patients, so a dialysis-dependent patient has a greater chance of dying before being readmitted. The direction of that bias is towards the null, so the reported association is, if anything, an underestimate.

Administrative coding defines every variable. Comorbidities, complications and the exposure itself are ICD-10 codes, not clinical observations. There is no present-on-admission indicator in any NRD data year in this window, so an index complication cannot be distinguished with certainty from a condition present at arrival, and every present-on-admission restricted analysis is not estimable in this data source (it is listed as such in Table 6). For the same reason prior major bleeding and prior stroke coded on the index record cannot be separated from a periprocedural event during the index stay. Coding intensity also increased across the study window, so an apparent increase in the prevalence of an any-listed condition reflects ascertainment as much as incidence.

The number of populated diagnosis and procedure fields differs across data years. Because the exposure requires an any-listed diagnosis together with an any-listed dialysis marker, it is ascertained less completely in years with fewer populated fields. The pre-specified sensitivity analysis that re-ascertains the exposure within the uniform field depth present in every year is reported in Table 6.

The device model cannot be identified. ICD-10-PCS code 02L73DK covers every intraluminal left atrial appendage occlusion device. The restriction to 2020-2022 discharges is therefore a calendar restriction, not a device restriction, and no comparison between device generations is possible from these data.

Dialysis vintage, modality and adequacy are unrecorded. The exposure is binary. Time on dialysis, haemodialysis versus peritoneal dialysis in a form reliable enough to stratify on, residual renal function and dialysis adequacy are all absent, and each is plausibly associated with both the decision to implant and the risk of readmission. Frailty is likewise unmeasured. The E-value quantifies how strong such a confounder would have to be.

Indication for the procedure is not recorded. Left atrial appendage occlusion is performed in patients judged unsuitable for long-term anticoagulation, and the reason for that judgement is not in the data. Dialysis-dependent patients may reach the procedure through a different clinical pathway from other patients. The pre-specified subgroup restricted to patients with prior major bleeding is the closest available approach to a like-for-like comparison, because both arms of that stratum carry a documented bleed.

Anticoagulant and antiplatelet therapy after discharge is not recorded. Post-implantation antithrombotic strategy differs between dialysis-dependent and other patients and is a plausible mediator of bleeding readmission that cannot be measured here.

No race, ethnicity or geographic identifiers. The NRD contains no race or ethnicity variable and no geographic identifier below the national level, so disparities in access to or outcomes after this procedure cannot be examined and regional variation cannot be described.

Residual confounding. This is an observational analysis of administrative data. Overlap weighting balances measured covariates only; it does nothing about unmeasured ones. The negative control outcome and the E-value are reported so that the reader can judge the plausibility of residual confounding rather than take an assurance on trust.

Subgroup and cause-of-readmission analyses are exploratory. The exposed arm contributes roughly 461 readmission events in total. That number, not the size of the full cohort, governs the precision of every stratified estimate, and it is why the cause-of-readmission table reports four categories rather than fifteen and why no subgroup finding appears in the Conclusions.

7 Anticipated statistical review

Prepared responses to the criticisms this analysis is most likely to attract. Each is answered from what was actually done, with the location of the supporting evidence.

“You have used an odds ratio for a common outcome, which exaggerates the effect.” Agreed, which is why the odds ratio is not the headline estimate. Table 3 reports the marginally standardized adjusted absolute risk in each arm, the adjusted risk difference in percentage points and the adjusted risk ratio, all obtained by g-computation over the observed covariate distribution with delta-method variance on the design-based covariance matrix. The abstract leads with the absolute risk difference.

“Your standard errors are wrong because you pooled seven years of NRD data.” Stratum and hospital identifiers are re-issued each data year and do not identify the same unit across years. Year-unique stratum and cluster identifiers were constructed before the design was specified, which prevents unrelated hospitals from collapsing into one cluster. Table S1 reports the resulting number of strata, primary sampling units and design degrees of freedom.

“You rebuilt the survey design for each subgroup, which discards strata.” We did not. A single design object was built once on the complete cohort and every analysis in this report, including every subgroup and every sensitivity analysis, is a subset() of that object. This is stated in the Methods and is visible in the analysis scripts.

“With this few exposed events you cannot support that many covariates.” Table 3c separates the two quantities this objection conflates. The stability of a logistic model’s coefficients is governed by the smaller of the event and non-event counts across the whole cohort, which here is in the thousands; the exposed-arm event count governs the precision of the exposure contrast and the granularity at which subgroups can be reported. The covariate block was kept compact for that reason, the full 31-flag Elixhauser set was deliberately not used, the overlap-weighted estimator reduces the outcome model to a single exposure term, and every subgroup and cause-of-readmission analysis is labelled exploratory.

“Renal failure is in your comorbidity index and also in your exposure.” It is not. The Elixhauser renal failure flag was removed from the comorbidity count by pre-specification, as was every comorbidity entered individually in the model, so the residual count double-counts nothing.

“This is confounding by indication: these patients were selected for the procedure differently.” Probably true in part, and it is stated as a limitation rather than argued away. Three things address it directly: the overlap-weighted co-primary estimate, which balances the measured covariate set exactly; the pre-specified subgroup restricted to patients with prior major bleeding, in which both arms carry a documented bleed; and the E-value, which states how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be.

“A Cox model would be more appropriate.” Every patient in the analytic cohort has complete 30-day follow-up by construction and the only censoring is administrative at day 30, so a hazard ratio adds nothing to a binary outcome. Cox is reported as a sensitivity analysis fitted on the full cohort with administrative censoring at day 30, never on readmitted records only.

“Your Kaplan-Meier curve ignores the competing risk of death.” The figure is labelled as cumulative incidence of first readmission among discharge survivors, not as survival. Post-discharge death is not observed in the NRD at all, so no competing-risk estimator can be fitted; the direction of the resulting bias is towards the null and is stated in both the figure legend and the Limitations.

“Length of stay should be in the model.” Length of stay and discharge disposition lie on the causal path between dialysis dependence and readmission. They appear only in Model 5 of Table 4, which is labelled as over-adjusted and is presented to demonstrate mediation. Model 4 is the primary specification.

“You have not adjusted for multiplicity.” The primary outcome is tested once and is the only confirmatory test. Secondary outcomes form one pre-specified Benjamini-Hochberg family whose membership was fixed before any result was seen; the cause-of-readmission categories form a second, separate family and the two are never pooled. Sensitivity analyses are consistency checks and are deliberately not corrected, which is stated where they are reported. Subgroups are exploratory and are not corrected, which is also stated.

“How do we know this is not just residual confounding?” A negative control outcome with no plausible causal link to the exposure was pre-specified and analysed with the identical model (Table 6b), and an E-value is reported on the risk ratio scale. Neither proves the absence of confounding and neither is presented as doing so.

“This has already been published.” Amin AM et al. Left atrial appendage occlusion in patients with chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease: a propensity-matched TriNetX analysis of 10,689 patients. European Heart Journal Open 2026. doi:10.1093/ehjopen/oeag082 reports a propensity-matched network analysis pooling chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease. This study differs in three ways that are stated in the Introduction rather than left for a reviewer to find: the exposure requires demonstrated dialysis dependence rather than a coded kidney-failure diagnosis, and the sensitivity analysis using the wider definition quantifies how much that requirement changes the estimate; the outcome is all-cause readmission to any hospital in a nationally representative all-payer sample rather than a convenience network; and the cause-of-readmission and hospital-volume analyses are not available in the comparator data source.

“Your cost figures are not comparable across years.” Charges were converted to costs using the HCUP hospital-specific cost-to-charge ratio and deflated to 2022 US dollars using CUUR0000SA0. The series identifier and its annual values are printed in this report so that the adjustment can be reproduced exactly.

All figures were produced in R with ggplot2 and are supplied as vector PDFs together with 600-dpi PNG copies in the figures/ directory. Vector artwork has no intrinsic resolution; the raster copies exist only for pasting into a word-processor draft and should not be submitted in place of the PDFs. Figures use shape and greyscale contrast rather than colour so that they remain readable in black-and-white print and to readers with colour vision deficiency. Cells suppressed under the HCUP minimum-cell rule are absent from the figures as well as from the tables, so no suppressed count can be recovered from a plotted value.
